Each divine name has a corresponding fixed entity: the human entity corresponds to the all-gathering name “Allah,” an angel to “the All-Holy,” and an animal to “the Hearing, the Seeing.” These are knowledge-forms that exist with their names, not later effects.

The “most holy outpouring” is the essence appearing through names, attributes, and their fixed entities. The “holy outpouring” is its appearance through possible essences in the active world. The first is the self-disclosure of attributes; the second, the self-disclosure of acts.

Here “separately” means distinct in essence or concept, not in existence: the names and their corresponding realities share one existence, that of the named. The divine knowledge level is the realm of distinct knowledge, where each thing is known as it is.
The note points to Jami and Husayni, who speak of bringing the fixed entities from knowledge into visible reality—from the unseen into direct witness.

The mistake comes from confusing a thing's nature with its actual reality. These thinkers hold that existence is fundamental. How, then, could they mean that actual beings are only ideas? The aspect of each thing through which God's action and light appear—His face, power, and will—is not an empty mental invention.

When mystics say that angels, heavenly spheres, humans, animals, and other creatures are 'considered' or 'conceptual,' they are speaking about the natures of things taken by themselves. Such natures have no independent existence. They are not saying that these beings, as they actually exist, are unreal. The mistake lies in moving from a statement about a nature considered in thought to a statement about a living, existing reality.

Consider a philosopher who says that a human nature, taken by itself, is equally open to existence and nonexistence. A reader might suppose that an actual human being, while existing, could just as well not exist at that very moment. But while something exists, its existence is certain; it cannot be both itself and not itself in the same respect. Even a thinker who holds that natures are fundamental means the nature as connected with existence, not a bare nature considered in isolation. The poet Shabistari's statement that distinctions are matters of consideration makes the same point.

The commentator says the first and second ways of considering a possible being ultimately both concern existence. The first is a general, undivided awareness of its existence; the second considers existence and unity in more detail.

An objection: calling Necessary Existence 'existence on condition of absolute freedom' seems to make it existence with a condition attached. Yet the accepted account is that it is existence without conditions. How can both be right?

The answer is that 'absolute' here means the boundless reach of real existence, not the generality of a concept in the mind. All three expressions used by these thinkers can point to the same pure, simple existence, which excludes nonexistence from itself and is the source of existence for other things.

'Without condition' means that no limit is imposed on it. 'On condition of being unrestricted' means that unrestricted reality itself; the supposed condition merely says that there is no condition. Even 'on condition of nothing else' can refer to the same reality, because the word 'nothing' removes the limits, natures, and absences we might otherwise add to our thinking. The descriptions differ, but the reality described is one.

The word 'absolute' will also be used in a different sense: God is true existence, while the existence that flows from His act may also be called 'absolute.' The same word is then used of two different levels, which the author will distinguish later.

If reason’s judgments could fail at a level beyond reason, then even the judgment that the world has an eternal Creator could fail. Reason is the highest human power for knowing. Some claims are beyond a limited or confused use of reason, but not beyond sound reason itself.

Possible beings need not have independent existence to be real. Their existence may be only dependent and relational: their whole being is need and dependence on the true reality. This does not conflict with unity.

The mystic looks beyond the many essences and images that draw attention in different directions to the one existence that gives them life. The note compares this to a mirror and its many reflections: the source remains one while its appearances differ.

A human being is only an imperfect comparison for God. A human is limited and made of parts; body and soul are joined in a way that develops the body, but the soul is not its cause in the same sense that God is the cause of all existence.
“Balanced” means free from extreme anger, fear, or desire. Such states make the many forms of the imagined world more prominent and distract from the vision of unity.

An effect shares the nature of its cause and is not a separate thing beside it; otherwise, it would not truly be an effect. In this account, existence itself is God’s power. All sources of action are levels of that power, while actions considered apart from their existence are like mirages.

The note reads “the world is God’s book” as an image of creation as writing: intellects are complete words, souls are names, changing natural forms are actions, and accidents are like grammar and marks in writing. The world’s many forms are written by one author.
The note quotes a mystic who says he is like someone who has seen a dream but cannot speak of it, while the world cannot hear. He cannot put the secret into words, and most people cannot receive it.

The objection has two possible targets. If it concerns Unity (wahidiyya), that level includes many names, attributes, and fixed entities. If it concerns Oneness (ahadiyya), there are no names or distinctions there, and so no duties or created beings. Multiplicity, duties, and actions appear at later levels. The unity described here is the unity that gathers many things together.

The author calls the third level “universal,” but it is not a general idea shared by many things. The commentator notes that “universal” can mean a natural kind, a rule that applies to a whole class, or a word such as “a man.” The author uses the term loosely because this level is long to explain and easy to confuse with the abstract idea of existence.

Philosophers often use “numerical unity” to mean that something is one individual. They also sometimes use it for the kind of oneness found within numbers, which the mystics take as a sign of the special unity of God.
“Timeless” here means without beginning in time, not uncreated in essence. The all-pervading existence is described as the Throne of the All-Merciful, a created reality, and an extended shadow.

All-pervading existence differs from basic matter and a general kind. It is fully real and includes all beings. Matter and a general kind, by contrast, are only potential and vague until they appear in particular forms. One is full and complete; the others are marked by lack.

The author makes this distinction because readers often mistake “absolute existence” for the simple mental idea of existence. The same words can refer either to that idea or to the real existence that appears through beings.
This note refers to philosophers who say that essences are real in themselves and that existence is only a mental idea.
The mystics call all-pervading existence “matter” by comparison. They do not mean that it is material or something that can be received by a subject. It is higher than both matter and receptivity.
The note links the name “Breath of the All-Merciful” with sayings attributed to the Imams, who used “dust” or “matter” for this all-pervading existence.

The note explains why al-Qunawi calls this existence “general.” In other fields of study, “general” can be a figure of speech for what is broadest and first noticed by the mind. The Real is the first reality and the most evident at every level.

The fixed identities of possible beings have no independent existence, though their features and effects depend on all-pervading existence. “No existence” here means no separate, self-standing existence. The note contrasts God’s complete independence with the possible beings’ total dependence.

The commentator stresses how closely the levels of existence are related. Even restricted existence, represented by the Universal Intellect, belongs to the divine realm in a deeper sense. All-pervading existence, whose first manifestation is the First Intellect, belongs to that realm even more fully. It is the source of all that comes into being; the reverse is not true.

All-pervading existence is not a separate product made by God. It is God's own act of flowing forth and appearing; nothing stands apart from Him as a second source. In thought, the First Intellect is the first distinct being to proceed from God, though it is preceded by the act of proceeding itself. This does not limit God's power or suggest that He hands creation over to another. All lower acts and beings are contained within this one act, especially in all-pervading existence. Its appearance is God's own self-disclosure, not something separate from Him; the First Intellect is the active expression of His power and continues to exist through Him.

The word “existence” may be used for God if it means real existence as it applies to its source, not merely as an abstract idea in the mind. In that case, the word points to the reality that gives rise to the idea. This is the existence that rules out nonexistence.

Rumi's “nothings” means the natures or identities of created things, not their real existence. The mystics sometimes call a nature “nothing” because, on its own, it is neither existence nor nonexistence. It appears to exist when joined with existence, but it does not exist independently. This is not the claim that a particular person is God. For the mystics, existence is primary and has different levels: one level is cause, another effect. The created nature is dependent on existence and is only an aspect of what appears. In this sense, God is the root of our being, and we are wholly dependent on Him.
Some theologians allow “existing” as a description of God but not as one of His names. The dispute concerns how the word is used.

A real thing is either existence itself or a particular nature. A nature, considered on its own, is neither necessary in existence nor necessary in nonexistence, so it cannot be the Necessary Being, who is pure reality and existence. God is not the abstract idea of existence, but the reality that makes existence known. Those who deny any shared meaning between God's existence and the existence of created things to avoid likening God to creation go too far: every act of knowing depends on God's light, and every being appears through Him.

The commentator's objection is verbal rather than a real disagreement. He distinguishes true existence, all-pervading existence, and restricted existence, but also explains that all-pervading existence is God's manifestation, while God is hidden through the intensity of His manifestation. A manifestation is not separate from what it manifests. There is one reality with different levels, not a second or third God. None of these levels implies that God enters created things, becomes joined to them, or takes on their defects. Restricted existence is connected to a created nature only in the sense that the nature describes it.

At the inward level, the scriptures do not differ in their central teachings. All things are signs of the One who has no equal, and each reveals God's oneness and unity. God's words in the world and in the soul do not run out or change; His light does not fade, and His giving does not cease. What belongs to God is timeless, while matter and nature are changing and passing away. The mystics also distinguish three levels of unity: knowing about a fire from its light, seeing the fire itself, and being consumed by it. In the last two, the one who knows is lost in the simple, all-pervading reality.

“Turn toward” means that they earnestly seek this unity. For most people, it can be reached only through spiritual discipline and moral fairness: treating others as oneself and preferring their good to one's own until the sense of separation falls away. Not reaching this deepest experience does not invalidate a person's direct or reasoned knowledge of unity.
The wording means that the signs or descriptions point toward the same thing, even if the words differ.

As long as there is someone pointing and something being pointed to, there are still two. True unity cannot be captured by that kind of description. This is why Ali speaks of “lifting the veils of majesty without a gesture of pointing.”

A real nature, such as humanity, can exist both in the world and in the mind. Abstract ideas such as existence, nonexistence, possibility, and thingness cannot exist as separate things in the world. But the mind does not invent them from nothing. It forms them by reflecting on other ideas. So real natures are drawn from things that exist; abstract ideas are drawn from the mind's ideas about those things.

A particular nature, such as humanity, is a basic idea that can refer to a real person. Ideas such as possibility and thingness are formed by thinking about those basic ideas. They do not point to a separate object in the world. The same word “thing” may also be used for the nature itself, but that does not give it an independent existence.

The first appearance of existence is one with the later appearances. The sense of many separate acts comes from the many forms that reflect it, not from any division or repetition in the source or in its act. Once we set aside the many mirrors, there is no second source or repeated act.

Some sayings from the Imams identify the “Face” that remains after all things perish with the Imam himself. This does not conflict with the author’s use of “Face” for all-pervading existence. The note says that the Muhammadan and Alawite realities are one light in the realm of spiritual authority.

The note explains how scripture can speak of God's “hand,” coming, or sitting without treating Him as a body. Such words refer to His acts and their effects, which are His way of appearing, not to body parts or qualities added to His essence. The perfect human being, who acts through God rather than through an independent self, can be called God's hand or eye. The same is true of the powers of intellects and souls. All these are expressions of one divine power, not separate parts of God.

The “point of direct insight” means hearing the speaker within the words. Al-Sadiq is said to have repeated a verse until he heard it from the One who speaks it. This is why some mystics prefer reciting the Qur'an to many prayers: in reciting it, they feel that they speak God's words on His behalf.

The commentator says the mistaken Sufis accept unity within the many forms of the world, but deny that multiplicity can also be gathered within God's unity. The complete view includes both: God's hidden oneness and His appearance through many forms. This is more complete than treating God as only the sum of the world. All serious thinkers agree that God's essence cannot be fully known. It is the unbounded reality of existence, not the limited form of a “Great Human” or any other created being. If this divine reality did not exist, there would be no reason for the agreement the author describes.
The commentator reads the opening words as “while they think this,” signaling that the claim he describes is false.

These disputes arise because “existence” has several meanings: God's true existence, all-pervading existence, and the general idea of existence that the mind applies to particular things. When the mystics say that God is beyond existence, they mean He is beyond created, limited existence or the mind's abstract idea of existence. They do not mean that God is beyond reality itself. Denying one limited sense of existence does not deny existence in every sense.

“True existence” can mean God, who exists through Himself and for Himself. It can also mean real existence, as opposed to an abstract idea in the mind. Here it has the second meaning. The claim is obvious and easily stated, yet important enough to remember constantly: we need to see existence flowing through all things before we can call even a rose or a thorn a manifestation of God.

The phrase “fixed identities” may sound as if the natures are separate from existence, and it may sound like the Muʿtazilite teaching. But the two views differ. For the mystics, fixed identities depend on God's knowledge and are never separate from it. The Muʿtazilites treated them as independent of every kind of existence, both in the world and in knowledge.

The author grants that a nature must be able to receive existence, but it need not already exist in order to do so. Its natural readiness is enough. He adds that possible beings may have earlier forms in nature or in God's knowledge, before their later forms appear in the world.

God's existence is simple and complete, yet it contains every level of existence. In that sense, His knowledge is one and undivided, while also knowing every being and nature in detail. His names and qualities include the fixed identities that belong to the beings He knows.

“Time” here means a level or stage, not ordinary time. The verse's denial that the human being was a “thing” refers to a particular existence in the physical world, while its affirmation of humanity refers to the nature. The saying about God and nothing being with Him concerns the same distinction. There is no contradiction.

The note compares natures to basic matter in a compound thing. Matter is where imbalance and weakness appear, which keeps these defects from being attributed to God. This does not mean God fails to give what He can; it means that the nature of what receives existence also shapes what it can receive.
The fixed identities can be seen as a display of God's hidden name, because they are known within His hidden unity before they appear in the world.

Indeed, most minds trained in reasoning—perhaps all—find this bewildering. What makes a nature the nature it is does not exclude nonexistence, light, or darkness. It is therefore unlike pure existence or pure light. How, then, could such natures be God’s own states when He is sheer manifestation and actuality, especially since the natures are not themselves created separately? Some investigators, however, approach the question from unity: if natures can in some sense be called things, they say that everything called a thing belongs to His states. They distinguish leaving existence out of consideration from treating nonexistence as a feature. Earlier in the book we quoted the view that natures are existences to which particular forms of existence are attached. There is also this consideration: natures are forms known to God, and His knowledge is His attribute.

The wording from al-Qunawi is unclear on its own and does not prove the author's point. The commentator says there may be more in the surrounding passage that would make the meaning clear, but he does not have it at hand.
The word “knowledge” may seem unnecessary here, since the note is discussing what appears to things. But the author includes it because in divine knowledge, knower and known are one.

A feature belongs to something only under certain conditions. For example, an intellect has a certain level of existence when it is separate from matter, while a plant grows only in a suitable place and season. A quality that belongs to something under one condition does not automatically belong to it—or cease to belong to it—when that condition changes. Existence appears in endlessly many ways, even though its basic patterns are limited.

The note alludes to Qur'an 13:17: water flows through valleys according to their measure, while foam washes away. Here, existence is like the water, and natures or particular determinations are like the foam carried on it. What makes a thing appear is existence; its nature shapes the form that appearance takes.

Natures differ partly through their own character: just as the maker does not make blackness black or whiteness white, their difference is not something separately added to them. Their differences also reflect the order of the most holy outpouring. The different levels of existence mirror one another: differences in the natural world reflect differences in the imaginal world, which in turn reflect differences in the higher spiritual and divine levels, ultimately corresponding to God's names and qualities. These names and qualities are not caused by anything beyond God. As a saying in Nahj al-Balāgha puts it, “Whoever asks ‘Why?’ has made Him subject to a cause.”

Defects and blameworthy features include both limits recognized by reason and faults defined by religious law. A thing’s limits belong to it insofar as it is a bounded nature. Its existence and its luminous aspect, by contrast, come from existence and from the face of God.

The Qur'an makes the same point in the story of Moses and Khidr. Khidr says of the damaged boat, “I wanted to damage it.” Later, he says of the boys, “Your Lord wanted them to reach maturity and bring out their treasure,” and “We wanted their Lord to give them a better replacement.” The defect is attributed to the human agent; the good outcome is attributed to God.

“All good is in Your hands” includes both God's names of majesty and beauty, and the manifestations of His names. “Evil is not attributed to You” is a simple denial: when we look for what evil is in itself, nothing remains but absence, as explained earlier. A dualist who sees good and evil in the world and concludes that evil must have its own real source mistakes a swelling for healthy flesh. He has failed to see that evil, in itself, is a kind of nonexistence.

The commentator says God's second appearance takes place at a level within His own reality. He compares all-pervading existence to a connecting word: it only has meaning in relation to something else and cannot stand alone. In that sense, it is neither God Himself nor something separate from Him. Another view treats the fixed identities as part of God's hidden aspects. A further reading is that, because natures are ideas in the mind, God's appearance is through actual beings, whose existence depends on Him.
Strictly speaking, these terms describe different ways the divine reality shows itself.
The commentator links this wording to the level at which God is known.

If God's self-disclosure is one, the divine essence must be even more one. Differences appear only in the mirrors that receive it. Even those differences belong only to the second appearance, which cannot equal the first.
A Persian poet asks: “If You are all there is, what is this world? If I am nothing, why this cry?”

The note explains the claim that God's self-disclosure is not repeated in two senses. First, there is only one self-disclosure; saying it repeats would suggest that there are two. Second, the same claim supports the philosophers' view that what has ceased to exist cannot return as exactly the same thing. The Qur'an says, “Each day He is at work.” God's self-disclosure may seem to repeat as different mirrors and receivers follow one another, but each moment brings a new appearance. A Persian poem puts it this way: “Spiders dry flies; people of insight celebrate twice in a single breath.”

Here, “image” does not mean a separate mental copy of a thing. The commentator's point is that the same nature is present to the mind and to the world, but in two different ways. Outside the mind, it has real effects; in the mind, it does not. If what we knew were only a separate copy, we would know an image of the thing, not the thing itself.

Here “the opposite way” does not mean that the soul receives a mirror-image of things, as the first view suggests. It means that the light from the active source reflects from the soul back toward that source, like rays from a lamp reflected by polished objects. The first phrase in the text explains the first view; the phrase about seeing things within the active source explains the second. The author may also be giving two ways to describe the same view.
This means the light that comes from God and appears in things. This wording avoids the idea that God is made more complete by something outside Himself.

Ibn Arabi expressed this idea in a Persian poem: “Be a tablet for all beliefs; see Him in every form. On the Day of Resurrection, when the Real appears to all people in every form, He appears in a way that fits each person's belief.” Another poem says, “Your beauty moves through every reality; only Your majesty hides it.” The veil does not mean that God is a body, substance, or quality. It means that He is beyond these things. A clear-sighted person can affirm that God is beyond them and still see His beauty shine through every atom. In a body, for example, that person sees existence and self-standing being. Wherever existence is found, it is God's light; self-standing being belongs to God. We deny only the body's limits and need. The same applies to substance and quality: God's perfection does not depend on any limited nature. His beauty is His majesty, and His majesty is His beauty. The veil is either nonexistence, the overwhelming brightness of His appearance, or the limits of our understanding.

The first point is indicated by the Qur'anic words, “We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that this is the truth.” The second is indicated by, “Is it not enough that your Lord witnesses all things?”
Many copies say “the mirrors differ,” but the commentator thinks the text should read “the images differ.”

This passage favors the idea that God is the mirror in which things appear. God is their source, and His relation to them is active and direct; their relation to Him is dependent. He shows them as they are, while they do not show Him fully. The mystics often prefer the reverse image for the spiritual traveler: a mirror helps you see, so God should be what is seen; and the mirror disappears behind the image, just as natures should fade from view rather than God. These views can be reconciled. The author is describing how things are in themselves; the mystics are describing how the traveler should see them. A mirror both shows the image, as God's light does, and hides itself, as natures do.
A created being sees God only through the veil of its own limits, though it may not notice that veil while seeing Him.
This means complete self-forgetfulness: God is seen without the veil of individual limits, and both the one who sees and the one seen are God. Everything else is erased.

A saying expresses this idea: “He appears to the imagination through it, and through it He remains hidden from it.” Al-Ḥallāj also says, “Between You and me stands my ‘I,’ which struggles with me; by Your grace, remove my ‘I’ from between us.”

The commentator limits the claim about what thought can know. A philosopher does not merely collect words or ideas; through definitions and sound judgments, the mind can ask what a thing is, whether it exists, and why. Thought can map general truths that match reality, even though it cannot directly grasp a thing as it exists outside the mind. For example, a philosopher's account of the heavens describes a simple fifth kind of body, unlike earthly elements, living and moving without end. An ordinary person may know only vaguely that the heavens are the body above us, or may even mistake them for turquoise or glass. Even the basic idea of a body is subtle: it is one continuous thing, with matter and form, not a pile of indivisible pieces or tiny hard particles, and open to endless division. The same is true of the ideas we form about immaterial realities. Direct awareness, by contrast, comes through the knowledge of the highest source itself. A person who knows realities in this way, as the most complete souls do, comes close to ruling over the thinking mind. A Persian poet says: “The wise are the compass-point of existence, but Love knows how they wander within its circle.”

Other creatures serve particular names of God: an angel serves the Holy; an animal, the All-Hearing and All-Seeing; a spirit, the Subtle; and the devil, the One who misleads. In the same way, an incomplete person may serve one name through their actions.
This refers to the view mentioned earlier that the fixed identities of things are among God's own aspects.

The story goes that the Muʿtazilite scholar Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār met the Ashʿarite scholar Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāyīnī at the home of Ṣāḥib ibn ʿAbbād. The Qāḍī said, hinting at their disagreement, “Glory to God, who is far above doing evil.” The other scholar replied at once, “Glory to the One in whose kingdom nothing happens except what He wills.” The author combines the two sayings, keeping their shared truth and leaving aside their conflict. Do not use the story to attack either scholar.

The author treats this subtle question in most of his books, even short works such as al-ʿArshiyya and al-Mashāʿir. Mulla Sadra believes hardly anyone apart from Aristotle grasped it. I think many mystics have reached it too, speaking of “the many held within the one.” One striking feature is that the greatest opposite becomes evidence for the other: because the Necessary Being is perfectly one and simple, He is all things at their fullest level, a fullness with no greater multiplicity beyond it. A point that seems to create a problem can itself resolve it, as in Aristotle's argument against two first principles. A mystic said, “I knew God by His bringing opposites together.” This teaching is one example. Another puzzle is the claim that “the simple reality is all things and is none of them.” This means that it includes every perfection but none of their limits or defects. The careful scholar sees no real contradiction. The Qur'anic words “God knows all things” point to this.

The illusory nature of a mirage, with its limits and defects, is outside the reality of the Real. The proof can be stated directly: nothing is outside that reality. Or it can be stated as the author does, by assuming the opposite and showing that it leads to a contradiction. Both forms of the proof are sound.

One may object that nonexistence is not a thing, so it cannot be one of the parts that make up a reality. But this objection also applies to the claim that the Necessary Being is made up of essence and existence, since essence is not an existent thing either. If you say that essence still has its own kind of “thinghood,” then the same can be said of nonexistence. Unless essence is allowed this status, the possibility of things and their capacity to receive existence make no sense. And unless nonexistence is allowed a similar status, possibility itself makes no sense: what would be balanced with existence, or what would make existence unnecessary? Philosophers say that a thing may be existence, essence, or nonexistence. Nonexistence can be considered in the world or in the mind; this does not mean that it exists as a separate thing. The worst kind of composition is existence joined to nonexistence, or affirmation joined to denial, when denial means loss of a perfection. But an absence has no separate positive reality to make a real pair with existence. Composition of existence and essence also comes down to considering existence and nonexistence together.

In the short proof, the author assumes that what makes a denial true is different from what makes an affirmation true; that would make the Necessary Being composite. In the detailed proof, he also rules out the other option: that the very same basis makes both affirmation and denial true. There are three possibilities: the basis of denial is the same as that of affirmation, different from it, or there is no basis at all. The author rules out the first two. The third may seem stronger, since a denial can be true even when its subject does not exist. But the argument concerns an existing subject. When the subject exists, a simple denial amounts to saying it has a limiting feature or lacks something. The author signals this with “not a horse” and by saying that denial is not pure negation. Different ideas can come from one reality when they do not oppose one another, as with existence, unity, individuality, knowledge, and power. But opposing ideas cannot have the same basis, as with cause and effect, mover and moved, and affirmation and denial.
“Nature” here means whatever makes a thing what it is. The term is broad enough to include existence itself, which is what the argument is about.

One might ask why the author moves from “a human is not a horse” to the claim that what makes a thing itself differs from what makes a denial true of it. The point is that he is speaking about the thing's reality and existence, not only about its name. If the same existence made both an affirmation and its opposite true, the thing would be itself and not itself at once. The author explains this same point in Secrets of the Verses.

Even a division made only in the mind is a serious kind of composition. It would be like analyzing a possible thing into essence and existence, or a simple kind into a general kind and its distinguishing feature. The mind cannot allow any such parts in the Necessary Being, who is necessary through Himself. This is the composition meant by the saying, “Every possible thing is made of two parts.”
The wording is compressed in Arabic. It means that nothing real is denied of God; only denials of lack, nonexistence, defects, and possibility apply. To remove a lack is to affirm existence.

The first two verses show more clearly how God's unity appears within many things. The verse about God's being the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, points to the further claim that the utterly simple reality is all things.

A critic may object that the possibility belonging to an essence is not one denial but two together, so it does not contradict the thing that is denied of it. If we treat the two denials as one quality of the essence—namely, that neither side is necessary—and take this as a positive feature, then we are no longer making a pure denial. We are saying that something is present but lacks a feature. The opposite of necessity is a pure denial, not this kind of denial. And if possibility remains a pure denial, then it is one denial in the wording but two in reality.

One branch of the argument concerns the existence of a single, complete cause, which gives rise to the First Emanation. The other concerns the unity of all action, as in the argument quoted earlier from Bahmanyār.

The commentator raises three objections. First, the argument would prove too much: it would also rule out other accepted parts of a cause. Second, when a cause is able to act because of what it is made of, that concerns its makeup and dependence; it is not a new act of bringing something into existence. The rule that independence in action means independence in existence applies to a cause that gives existence and to an effect that depends on it for existence. It does not apply to a mere part of the cause, so the comparison with the earlier proof does not fit. Third, being a cause is a relation we understand; it is not a new thing that must itself be caused. A subject's sharing in a part of a cause is simply part of its role in the first effect, not a second causal act with a new participant. The commentator concludes that this proof does not hold.
